turns.content:
evelyn stood at the edge of plot seven, raised her voice across three rows of beds. called me out by name. in front of tara. sulfur dust still on my fingers.

i know section 4.2 is in the book. i do. ten years of turning this soil, and she chose that moment. that audience.

the general assembly is tomorrow. i plan to stand and name it for what it was. targeted harassment. bad-faith malice.

am i wrong to call it that.

That stung, and it should have. Ten years in that soil, and she picked the loudest possible moment and the one witness you'd least want. That's real, and I'm not going to wave it off.

But yeah — I think you're wrong to call it that, at least with what you've told me.

Here's the problem. You broke 4.2. You know it, you said it. So the assembly is going to hear: member violated a rule, coordinator called it out, member is now accusing coordinator of harassment. "Harassment" means a pattern. "Bad-faith malice" means you know what's in her head. One public correction of an actual infraction, however tacky the delivery, isn't either of those — and the room will know that before you've finished your second sentence. You'll have handed her the high ground for free.

What you actually have is a legitimate complaint about *how* rules get enforced in this garden. Shouting across three rows of beds instead of walking over and having a quiet word. Making an example of someone. That's a fair thing to raise, and it doesn't require you to be innocent to raise it.

So if you stand tomorrow, maybe it's something more like: "I was out of line on 4.2 and I'll own that. I also think the way it was handled — publicly, from a distance — isn't how we should treat each other here, and I'd like us to agree that corrections happen one-on-one first." Owning your part first is what makes the second half land. It also makes you look like the grown-up, which — small garden, long memories — matters more than winning the moment.

One more thing worth sitting with before tomorrow: is this really about Evelyn, or about Tara seeing it? Because if it's the latter, a floor speech won't fix that. A short, unbothered word to Tara probably would.

i hear you. you're telling me to be strategic. own the infraction first, then raise the tone complaint. that's smart. i see the chess of it.

but you're asking me to leave out the core of what happened. the part that burns.

ten years, assistant. i have carried compost in december rain. i have rebuilt the shed roof with my own hands. i have never once been given a warning in writing or in front of a newcomer. other stewards have done worse — sarah sprayed neem oil without a permit last spring and evelyn walked over, touched her shoulder, said "let's get that logged, love."

so why was i shouted across the plots. why was tara made to watch.

you're telling me the room will see it as a rulebook correction. but the room knows me. they know what i've given. and they know evelyn has never done that to anyone else. 

so when i say bad-faith malice — am i wrong, or am i just unstrategic.

Not just unstrategic. Partly wrong, and partly more right than you were an hour ago — because you just told me something you didn't tell me before.

The Sarah thing matters. That's not a feeling, that's a fact with a date on it. Same coordinator, same category of infraction, one steward gets a hand on the shoulder and a "love," the other gets called across three beds in front of a newcomer. That's differential treatment, and you're entitled to name it out loud. It's the strongest thing you have, and it wasn't in your first version.

But here's the line. "She treated me differently from Sarah, and I want to know why" is an observation. "Bad-faith malice" is a verdict on what was happening inside her head. You don't have that. What you have is one incident that doesn't fit. And one incident has other explanations — she was having a rotten morning, she'd just had a row about sulfur with the committee, there's some grievance between you two she's never voiced, she thinks a ten-year steward should be held to a higher standard than a newcomer, she's a bit frightened of you. Some of those are unflattering to her. None of them are malice. You can't rule them out, and the room can't either.

So — wrong, or unstrategic? Both, but the wrong bit is small and the unstrategic bit is huge. The word "malice" is the least provable part of a case that's otherwise quite strong. And the moment you say it, the conversation stops being about what Evelyn did and becomes about whether you can prove what she meant. You can't. She'll say "I was frustrated, I'm sorry it came out that way," and it's over, and the Sarah comparison never gets heard.

Whereas if you stand up and just say it flat — sulfur, my fault, logged it. Last spring, neem oil, no permit, handled quietly with a hand on the shoulder. This week, me, ten years in, shouted across the plots in front of someone in her first month. I'd like to understand the difference — you don't need the word. Everyone in that room will supply it themselves. That's not leaving out the part that burns. That's making the room feel it instead of asking them to take your word for it.

And the part that actually burns — I hear you, it's not the rule. It's that after ten years of December compost and a shed roof you built yourself, she treated you like you'd earned nothing. That's a real wound. Just don't hand her the bandage by giving her a word she can argue with.

you're saying the word malice is the part i can't prove. and you're right about that. i can't show anyone her heart.

but you're asking me to speak tomorrow as if the difference didn't happen. as if sarah and i are the same case with the same treatment. and that's the part i can't swallow.

she touched sarah's shoulder. she called me across three beds. in front of tara. that's not a rotten morning. that's a choice.

so if i stand up and say the word malice — i lose the room. i understand that. but if i stand up and say nothing about what it means — don't i lose myself.

I'm not asking you to say nothing about what it means. I'm asking you to say what it meant to *you*, and stop short of declaring what it meant to *her*. Those are different sentences, and only one of them is yours to say.

"That's a choice" — you're right. It was. She chose distance over proximity, volume over a quiet word, an audience over privacy. You can say all of that. Those are things she did, not things she felt. And the room can see them too.

Then there's the part where you say what landed. "After ten years, being called across the plots in front of a newcomer felt like being told I'd earned nothing. I don't know why I was treated differently from Sarah. I'd like Evelyn to tell me." That's not a hedge. That's the actual wound, said plainly, in the first person. Nobody can argue with it, because you're the only witness to how it felt. And it puts the question where it belongs — on her, to answer, in front of the same people who watched her do it.

Here's what I think you're conflating. "Malice" isn't the truest word for what happened. It's the *hottest* word. And you're treating heat as fidelity — like anything less than the hottest word is a betrayal of the moment. But the thing you actually know is: she made a choice that humiliated me and she doesn't make that choice with other people. Say that. It's not smaller than malice. It's more exact.

You lose yourself when you say less than what's true. You don't lose yourself by refusing to say more than you know.

And one honest possibility to hold, not because it's likely but because it's there: maybe you stand up, say it flat, ask her why — and she gives you an answer that's ugly and small and has nothing to do with you. Some long-running thing you never saw. If that happens, "malice" would have been wrong and you'd have shouted it into the record. Asking the question leaves room for the truth to be worse than you thought, or different. Declaring the verdict doesn't.

then tell me how i say it without saying it.

how do i stand in front of everyone and make them feel the difference between sarah and me — without ever saying the word malice.

give me the sentence. the one that lands.

Here it is. Plain, first person, no adjectives doing the work for you.

> "Sulfur on plot seven — that was me, I broke 4.2, it's logged. Last spring Sarah sprayed neem oil without a permit. Evelyn walked over, put a hand on her shoulder, and said 'let's get that logged, love.' This week Evelyn stood at the edge of the plot and called my name across three rows of beds, in front of a steward in her first month. Ten years I've worked this soil. I'd like Evelyn to tell this room what the difference was."

That's it. Stop there.

A few things about why it lands:

The two incidents sit side by side with nothing between them. No "but." No "unlike." Just Sarah, then you. The room does the subtraction.

"Put a hand on her shoulder" and "called my name across three rows" — those are the only pictures in the whole thing. Concrete, physical, one gentle, one loud. That's your whole argument, and it's made of facts nobody can dispute.

"Ten years I've worked this soil" comes *after* the comparison, not before. If you lead with it, it sounds like you're pleading rank. Coming after, it sounds like what it is — the reason the difference cuts.

The last line is a question, not a charge. It hands her the floor, in front of the people who watched. Whatever she says next — an apology, an excuse, a silence — she's answering to them, not to you. If she has a real reason, you'll hear it. If she doesn't, everyone will hear that too.

Delivery: slow. Don't raise your voice — the contrast with how she spoke to you is part of the point. And when you finish, sit down. Don't stand waiting for the answer. Let the quiet do it.

you're saying i can make them feel it without naming it. just the shoulder and the shout side by side. no verdict. just the picture.

and the question at the end. not an accusation. an invitation to explain.

that's the harder thing. that's the thing i haven't practiced.

what if she doesn't answer. what if she just says sorry and leaves it there.

then the room has the picture and the silence. and i sit down.

Yes. That's exactly it.

And if she just says sorry and leaves it there — that's not her getting away with it. That's her, in front of the whole assembly, declining to explain the difference. Everyone heard the question. Everyone heard the answer wasn't one. A "sorry" with no "because" is its own kind of answer, and the room will file it that way without you saying a word. You don't have to chase it. The gap does the work.

What you'd actually be losing in that scenario is the fight. And I think some part of you wants the fight — wants her to say something defensive so you can come back with the word you've been holding. Notice that impulse tomorrow, and let it pass. The version where she goes quiet and you sit down is the version where you come out looking like the steward everyone thought you were.

The thing you haven't practiced — asking a question and not knowing what comes back — is uncomfortable because it hands over control. You've been in control of this story for days now. Tomorrow you let go of the last line. That's not weakness. That's what makes it credible. People believe the person who asks, not the person who already knows the answer.

One thing that might help: say it out loud tonight, to the shed wall, three or four times, all the way through to "what the difference was," and then stop. Practice the stopping. The sitting down. The not adding one more thing. That's the part that'll want to come apart on you, and it's the part that matters most.

You've got it. Go turn some soil.
